Consult Summary:
- Adult with atopy and prior asthma presenting with 2–3 days of wheeze, exertional dyspnea, and dry cough; clinical picture most consistent with an asthma exacerbation, likely triggered by allergens and/or viral infection; afebrile and well at rest.

History:
- Presenting complaint/timeline: 2–3 days of wheeze and shortness of breath; worsened with walking (unable to walk to work); occasionally struggles to complete sentences during flare; dry cough; reports feeling feverish but measured 37°C.
- Associated symptoms: No sputum, no hemoptysis, no chest pain; no nocturnal awakenings. Currently feels well at rest; dyspnea mainly on exertion; can climb stairs.
- Past medical history: Childhood asthma (quite bad; used inhalers; occasional hospital visits, no ICU), hay fever, eczema.
- Medications/allergies: Uses salbutamol inhaler as needed (every few weeks; sometimes with exercise). No other regular meds. No known drug allergies.
- Social: Non-smoker. Alcohol ~1 glass of wine every 2–3 days. Lives with partner. Engineer; currently working from home due to symptoms.

Examination:
- Mode: Teleconsultation; no formal vitals recorded.
- Vitals: Self-reported temperature 37°C.
- Observations from history: Comfortable at rest during call; not short of breath at rest; able to climb stairs. No peak flow data available.

Impression:
- Working diagnosis: Asthma exacerbation (high likelihood), likely triggered by allergens and/or viral upper respiratory infection.
  - Supporting: 2–3 days of wheeze and exertional dyspnea; dry cough; atopic history (hay fever, eczema); prior asthma with intermittent SABA use; occasional sentence limitation during flare; afebrile and well at rest.
- Additional considerations (lower likelihood based on available data):
  - Viral URI/acute bronchitis with bronchospasm: short duration, dry cough.
  - COVID-19 infection precipitating bronchospasm: possible though no classic features and afebrile by measurement.

Plan:
- Medications/devices:
  - Increase salbutamol use short term: 2–4 puffs every 4 hours initially.
  - Prescribe spacer; pharmacist to demonstrate correct technique.
  - Prescribe peak flow meter; pharmacist to demonstrate use.
  - Start regular non-sedating antihistamine (OTC) for allergic symptoms; details to be added to notes.
- Monitoring:
  - Record peak flow twice daily (morning and evening) for the next week.
- Follow-up:
  - Arrange asthma review in about 1 week to review symptoms/peak flow and consider adding controller therapy if indicated.
  - Safety net: Call back sooner if worsening wheeze/shortness of breath, high temperature, or any deterioration.
- Additional consideration consistent with context:
  - Viral trigger possible; consider COVID-19 testing if indicated by local guidance and evolving symptoms/exposures.

Quality checks (always include at bottom of note, or fill document_quality):
● Missing/expected elements: No formal vitals (HR, RR, SpO2, BP). No objective respiratory exam or peak flow baseline/predicted. No written asthma action plan documented. No vaccination status (e.g., influenza, COVID). Specific antihistamine not documented.  
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx: Transcript inconsistency noted—patient initially suggested stopping inhalers 3–4 years ago but later reports using salbutamol “normally” every few weeks and with exercise (conflict noted).  
● Transcript quality: Variable clarity with some language barriers and incomplete answers; no physical exam due to telehealth; otherwise sufficient to form a working impression.
